highlights:
Fireworks serverless is usually the simpler choice for bursty or uncertain traffic because you pay for input, cached-input, and output tokens. Fireworks on-demand can be cheaper when one or more dedicated GPUs stay sufficiently busy, but the answer depends on the GPU shape, model throughput, replica schedule, cache share, service tier, and whether the workload is eligible for batch processing. Fireworks describes serverless as per-token and on-demand deployments as per-GPU-time billing; the current pricing page lists H100 and H200 capacity at $8.00 per GPU hour, or $0.134 per GPU minute, before any region premium. results.title: Fireworks AI Pricing in 2026: Every Serverless Model Priced
results.author: DeAI Newsroom
highlights:
Fireworks serves 12 serverless models priced per token as of 2026-11-03 — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at $0.30/$1.20 with $0.006 cached input, Kimi K3 at $3.00/$15.00.

...

Fireworks's serverless card lists 12 models as of 2026-11-03, from Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B at $0.05/$0.20 to Kimi K3 at $3.00/$15.00. Cached input bills at half price or better, Batch mode halves everything, and Spot knocks 30% off.

Fireworks AI prices 12 models on its self-serve serverless rate card as of 2026-11-03, spanning $0.05/$0.20 per million tokens for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B A3B to $3.00/$15.00 for Kimi K3 — and its $0.006 cached-input rate on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is the deepest published cache discount among the hosts DeAI tracks.

...

- The serverless card is 12 rows, priced input/cached-input/output: Kimi K3 at $3.00 / $0.30 / $15.00, Qwen 3.8 Max at $2.00 / $0.25 / $6.00, GLM 5.3 at $1.40 / $0.26 / $4.40, Muse Spark Open at $1.25 / $0.15 / $4.25, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at $0.30 / $0.006 / $1.20, MiniMax M3 at $0.30 / $0.06 / $1.20, gpt-oss-120b at $0.15 / $0.015 / $0.60, GLM 5.3 Flash at $0.15 / $0.03 / $0.50, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B A3B at $0.05 / $0.01 / $0.20 (Fireworks pricing, accessed 2026-11-03).
- Every open-weight row carries a cache discount: GLM 5.3 Flash caches at 80% off, gpt-oss-120b and MiniMax M3 at 90% off, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 98% off ($0.006 versus $0.30) — cached input "bills at half price or less, with no write fee" per the pricing page (Fireworks pricing).
- Mode levers stack: Batch mode bills at 50% of Standard on input and output, Spot Serverless takes 30% off Standard uncached prices for retry-tolerant traffic, and Priority runs at a 25% premium — all on the same endpoint (Fireworks Serverless Modes).
- Rate limits are adaptive and per model: small models (under 800B parameters) reach ceilings of 216M Total Prompt TPM, 54M Uncached TPM, 2.16M Generated TPM at the top spending tier, with +25% steps every 15 minutes and a 72-hour idle reset (Fireworks rate limits).
- Third-party speed: Artificial Analysis measures DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (non-reasoning) at 418 tokens/s — the fastest of Fireworks's 12 listed models — and the provider's cheapest blended price is $0.04/M on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning BF16 (Artificial Analysis, accessed 2026-11-03).
- Retention is policy, not attestation: the privacy notice (last modified September 16, 2026) states no training on prompts without explicit opt-in and no logging of prompt or generation data for open models without opt-in; the Response API retains conversation data up to 30 days when `store=True` (Fireworks privacy notice; Zero Data Retention docs).

...

Fireworks AI is a Redwood City inference provider that serves open-weight and closed models per-token on shared serverless capacity, by GPU-second on On Demand deployments, or via Reserved Throughput — dollars-per-minute reservations backed by a 99.9% uptime SLA. The same endpoint speaks Standard, Priority, Fast, Batch, and Spot modes, which is the structural difference from hosts like Cerebras, whose card is fixed: on Fireworks, the mode you select per request changes the bill. The platform also sells GPU time (H100/H200 at $8.00/hour, B200 at $13.00, B300 at $15.00, GB300 at $20.00) and trains models, but this page prices the serverless token card, which is what most builders touch.

...

Every open-weight serverless model, Standard mode, first-party list rates accessed 2026-11-03. Closed models included for comparison (Ember-1, Rune):

Two structural notes the table hides. First, US-only capacity is a 50% premium on every model except Muse Spark Open, where it's waived — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (US) runs $0.45/$0.009/$1.80 versus $0.30/$0.006/$1.20. That's the price of a US-residency guarantee, and it's the cheapest one on this card by a wide margin. Second, models not on the card are priced by size: $0.10 per million tokens under 4B parameters, $0.20 for 4B–16B, $0.90 above 16B, and $0.50–$1.20 for MoE architectures — with one flat rate covering input and output and no separate cached-input discount. A fine-tune you upload therefore lands on a predictable, if undifferentiated, price.

Priority mode adds 25% across the board ($3.75/$0.375/$18.75 on Kimi K3, $0.375/$0.0075/$1.50 on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) in exchange for peak-load priority; Kimi K3 Fast runs a further 50% above Standard at $4.50/$0.45/$22.50. A decision-oriented row exists too: Rune 26B-A4B, a "System One" model that never generates output tokens, bills $0.042 input / $0.0084 cached / zero output — you pay for input only.

...

The card reflects a fast-moving catalog: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is listed as a separate ... from the base Flash (same price), Nemotron 3 Ultra is still labeled Preview, Qwen 3.8 Max and ... 1 sit at the ... end, and Spot Serverless is available only on select models (GLM ... 5.3, Kimi ... 3, and both DeepSeek V4.1 Flash variants on the published spot table). Prices move — the price-index deltas DeAI has published through October 2026 record repeated repricings across this field — so treat every figure here as dated to 2026-11-03 and re-verify against Fireworks pricing before committing spend.

results.title: Fireworks expands European capacity With NVIDIA | Fireworks
highlights:
NOV 03, 2026

# Fireworks expands European capacity with NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell platforms

At its inaugural Fireworks Forge conference, the company introduces Ultrafast for interactive applications, new cost efficiencies for long-running agents, and higher rate limits.

Fireworks, the platform for specialized intelligence, today announced an expanded collaboration with NVIDIA. Fireworks will expand its capacity in Europe with NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell Platforms. The planned expansion will also leverage the NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking for leading performance and throughput per watt. At Fireworks Forge, its inaugural user conference, the company also introduced new capabilities spanning enterprise inference workloads: an Ultrafast inference preview for interactive applications that need immediate responses, multi-day prompt caching and background mode for long-running agents, and higher rate limits to support growing demand.

...

This NVIDIA accelerated computing footprint will support deployments across Europe beginning in 2027. The added capacity will help Fireworks meet growing regional demand for open and specialized models as enterprises move more production AI onto the platform. The expansion builds on Fireworks’ work with NVIDIA to optimize inference for enterprise workloads, connecting accelerated computing with the software and model expertise companies need to run their own specialized intelligence.

...

- Fireworks helps customers accelerate latency-sensitive workloads with Fireworks Ultrafast, now in public preview on the NVIDIA Blackwell Platform. Leveraging NVIDIA’s full-stack accelerated computing platform with over 1000 co-designed domain-specific libraries, AI models, and tools such as CUDA-X, Nemotron, and Nsight, Ultrafast combines faster model computation with efficient communication across GPUs to support responsive, real-time AI applications, achieving inference speeds exceeding 1,500 tokens per second.
- Multi-day prompt caching and background mode for long-running agents. Multi-day prompt caching reduces the cost of reusing large amounts of shared context across repeated model calls. Background mode dramatically lowers inference costs for work that can run without an immediate response. Together, these capabilities make it more economical for agents to keep working in the background over extended periods.
- Higher rate limits and sub-minute cold starts to support growing demand. Increased limits give customers more room to scale both interactive applications and background agent workloads.

results.title: OpenRouter Pricing: 5.5% Fee vs Together, Fireworks [2026]
results.author: Tom Vance
highlights:
The timing matters. Meta’s Muse Spark Open landed on Together AI on October 15 and on Fireworks AI on October 20, and OpenRouter rebuilt its default provider routing on October 28. Each event changed what a million tokens costs in practice. The gap between sticker price and invoice is where these three platforms differ most.

...

## Fireworks AI Pricing: Standard, Priority, Spot and Batch

Fireworks advertises pay-per-token usage from $0.05 per million input tokens, with no commitment. The base rates track Together’s closely, but Fireworks stacks several tiers on top. Standard is the default. Priority raises the price in exchange for faster, more reliable capacity. Spot cuts 30% off Standard on best-effort capacity for select models. Batch cuts 50% off input and output for jobs that do not need an immediate answer.

The Priority premium is not a flat markup. Working from Fireworks’ published rates, it adds 25% on Ember-1, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 20% on GPT-OSS 120B, and 50% on Muse Spark Open and Qwen 3.8 Max. Spot works the other way. The page warns that throughput can drop to zero, so retry or fall back to Standard. Kimi K3 under Spot lands at $2.10 input and $10.50 output, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash lands at $0.21 and $0.84.

...

For raw GPUs, On-Demand pricing is reportedly $13 per hour for a B200 180GB and $15 for a B300 288GB. That is well above Together’s reported $8.99 for a B200, though the two companies may bundle different software, so do not read it as a like-for-like gap. Anyone choosing between hosted Qwen and Meta’s model can start from the Muse Spark Open versus Qwen3.8 agent benchmark before pricing either one here.

...

1. Day-zero hosting of Muse Spark Open. Together announced the model live on October 15 with a 1-million-token context window. Fireworks followed on October 20 on US serverless capacity and waived its 50% US-only premium for the model. A buyer who needed US processing paid 25% more on Together and nothing extra on Fireworks.
2. OpenRouter’s routing rebuild. On October 28 the router moved from price-first selection to a balance of price, latency, reliability and retry cost. Teams that never pinned a provider saw their effective rates shift without a pricing-page change. Secondary coverage reportedly put the increase near 6%, unconfirmed by OpenRouter.
3. Together pruning its serverless list. A PricingSaaS tracker reported that by October 26 Together had dropped four serverless models: Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, Llama 3.3 70B and MiniMax M2.7. Anyone hard-coding a model ID needs a fallback plan, because catalog entries disappear on a few weeks’ notice.
4. Together’s Post-Training launch. On October 19 Together introduced reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning for open-weight models including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8-27B, with a promotional GPU rate valid through December 14.
5. Fireworks’ Forge announcements. On November 3 Fireworks reportedly introduced an Ultrafast inference preview, multi-day prompt caching, a background mode, higher rate limits and added European capacity on NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell platforms. Multi-day caching, if priced like today’s cached input, would stretch the discount the table above shows.
6. ElevenLabs on OpenRouter. On October 7 OpenRouter added nine text-to-speech models and two speech-to-text models from ElevenLabs, with a 50%-off introductory promotion that ran through October 19. That promotion has ended, so current pricing is the standard rate. The move shows the router expanding past text.

results.title: Fireworks AI on socnet
highlights:
Dossier continued for Fireworks AI (part 1/4): Priority costs roughly 20–58% more than Standard, Fast costs 50% more, and batch inference

Dossier continued for Fireworks AI (part 1/4): Priority costs roughly 20–58% more than Standard, Fast costs 50% more, and batch inference bills at 50% of serverless pricing. Spot serverless, a separate offering for workloads that tolerate temporary capacity limits, costs 30% less than Standard and returns a 503 when no capacity is available rather than falling back. Embeddings bill on input tokens only, with rates by model size starting at $0.008 per million tokens for models up to 150 million parameters. ## On-demand GPUs and fine-tuning On-demand deployments bill per GPU-second: published rates cited in 2026 coverage are about $8 an hour for H100 and H200, $13 for B200, $15 for B300, and $20 for GB300, roughly double the bare-metal price of capacity providers like Crusoe — the gap is the managed, optimized, SLA-backed platform, not the hardware. Region-restricted deployments add about 50%. Fine-tuning covers supervised fine-tuning and preference tuning (SFT and DPO) priced per million training tokens, and a fine-tuned model serves at base-model rates. The catch developers complain about, documented by competitors, is model retirement: Fireworks removes serverless models in waves — Llama 3.3 70B in May 2026, gpt-oss-20B in August, GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 in September 2026 — so a production system pinned to a retiring model must migrate, and a dedicated deployment scaled to zero answers 503 while it wakes.

results.title: The hidden math behind inference provider pricing - airtrain.ai
results.author: AI research
highlights:
Fireworks AI and Together AI occupy a middle layer in the AI inference market. These companies provide specialized models and handle systems work like batching and quantization. Fireworks AI, which raised $1.505 billion in July 2026, serves more than 10,000 enterprise customers. The company processes over 40 trillion tokens daily. President George Hu, who held leadership roles at Salesforce and Twilio, joined the company. Fireworks AI targets enterprise workflow budgets by offering reinforcement fine-tuning to improve models for specific jobs. A tuned agent that reliably completes a multi step workflow can replace manual operations, BPO labor, or a seat based software module, which is a much larger budget bucket than a simple API call. This capability differs from Replicate, which focuses on simple deployment. While Replicate focuses on deployment, Together AI and Fireworks sell performance and catalog breadth. Providers in this category use token pricing for shared inference and capacity pricing for dedicated deployments. This provides an alternative to GPU clouds like RunPod or Lambda, where users manage their own hardware and operational headaches.

...

Published pricing data contains significant errors that distort cost comparisons. Fireworks prints Standard and Priority as adjacent columns in a single table. If a user selects the wrong column, every published number is 50% high. This defect makes it difficult to compare providers without checking specific tiers. In 2026, the market shows extreme price volatility. OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol maintains a promotional price of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens through November 21, 2026. Google scheduled a price increase for Gemini 3.8 Flash on January 1, 2027. The spread between the most expensive and least expensive options reached 100 to 1. Do not trust a token price scraped from a landing page. Batch processing is not always half the cost, as batch output rates vary across different models. Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. DeepSeek provides off-peak discounts, charging half price outside of peak hours. Why do providers continue to publish inaccurate pricing tables?

results.title: DeepSeek's cheap new model is making GPU scarcity ...
results.author: Julian Lim
highlights:
On October 20, DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference engine it uses to run V4.1-Flash in production, and the numbers it disclosed are the real story. A single cluster running the framework processes 155 trillion tokens a day and generates roughly $38 an hour per GPU at off-peak pricing, according to data highlighted by Latent.Space's AI News roundup. A third-party researcher cited in that analysis put hardware-level gross margins on that revenue at somewhere between 84% and 96%, before accounting for R&D, bandwidth, or operations. That is an extraordinary return per chip. And it is exactly why demand for the chips themselves isn't easing.

V4.1-Flash itself came out September 10, a 552-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model built on what DeepSeek calls a causal encoder-decoder design. Only about 8 billion parameters activate per token on input and 16 billion on output, and DeepSeek says the architecture cuts key-value cache requirements to roughly a quarter of its predecessor's memory footprint. The practical result: a typical request with 100,000 input tokens and 20,000 output tokens costs around five cents to run, at DeepSeek's own posted price of $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens, according to pricing data from LLM-Stats. The October 17 V4.1-Flash-1017 update is the top-ranked open-weight system on the Vals Index. V4.1-Flash scored 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1, tied with Claude Opus 5.5's lab-reported result and ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol's 72.7.

...

One-year H100 rental rates climbed from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, according to SemiAnalysis's index, launched in April from surveys of more than 100 industry participants. The Information subsequently reported that the index reached $2.60 by mid-June. SemiAnalysis attributes the jump to capacity that is effectively sold out across neoclouds, the specialized GPU rental firms that have taken on heavy debt to buy chips ahead of demand. That financing structure is precisely why investors have grown nervous. Neoclouds borrowed against future utilization. A cluster sitting idle can't service its debt.

V4.1-Flash doesn't change that math by competing for the same scarce chips in a vacuum. It changes it by making inference cheap enough that far more of it gets run. DeepSeek's own model is now live across 21 third-party inference providers, including Fireworks AI, Together AI, DeepInfra, Baseten, Novita, and Parasail, according to pricing comparisons tracked by Artificial Analysis. On Artificial Analysis's 7:2:1 blended pricing measure, Fireworks stands at $0.24 per million tokens, Together AI at $0.32, DeepInfra at $0.61, and DeepSeek at $0.26, with the providers also competing on throughput. That's a lot of competing infrastructure chasing the same workload. Every one of those providers needs GPU-hours to serve it.

highlights:
Fireworks opened Ultra-fast in preview on November 3 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. The mode trades a higher token bill and lower rate limits for faster generation.

## The same token mix costs more

The published standard prices for the same 1017 model are $0.30 per million uncached input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens. Its cached-input price is $0.006 per million. Each corresponding Ultra-fast rate is exactly eight times higher. For a hypothetical workload containing one million uncached input tokens and one million output tokens, the token bill is $12 instead of $1.50. That calculation holds token counts fixed; it is not a measured coding task or a claim about how many attempts an agent needs. Cache hits reduce the absolute input charge, but the eightfold ratio also applies to cached tokens. For this hypothetical fixed workload, shortening completion by one minute would cost an extra $10.50 for that minute saved. The pricing table also lists no Priority option for Ultra-fast.

highlights:

# AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at

Paul Nugent

Nov 4, 2026

AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

This is the most important AI infrastructure pricing story of the year, and the signal is unmistakable.

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

The critical detail: Trainium pricing is unchanged.

AWS now operates two parallel compute economics tracks:

🔹 NVIDIA TRACK: +20% — you absorb Nvidia's pricing power, supply constraints, AND AWS's margin protection layered on top.

🔹 TRAINIUM TRACK: flat — Amazon subsidizes the economics because every workload that migrates to Trainium deepens lock-in to the AWS ecosystem.
